summary: Updates the Enhanced Security Services for S/MIME so the structure linking a certificate to a signature is not hardwired to SHA-1. It defines a new attribute allowing algorithm agility. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Lets an email's signature use a newer fingerprint method instead of being stuck with an old one.

questions: why replace sha-1 in s/mime signatures
subtitle: Lets S/MIME signatures name their certificate with any hash algorithm instead of being stuck with SHA-1.

tldr.problem: The ESSCertID structure from RFC 2634 ties a signature to its signing certificate by a hash, but it was hardwired to SHA-1, and recent attacks on SHA-1 made that a problem.
tldr.mechanism: A new signed attribute, SigningCertificateV2, holds ESSCertIDv2 structures that include a hash algorithm identifier, defaulting to SHA-256. The old SigningCertificate attribute stays for SHA-1.
tldr.outcome: Signers can pick the hash used to identify certificates, and legacy implementations keep working. SigningCertificateV2 MUST be used for any algorithm other than SHA-1.

today: RFC 5035 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2007 that updates RFC 2634. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem With a Hardwired Hash
sections.content:
In the Enhanced Security Services (ESS) for S/MIME document, RFC 2634, a structure called ESSCertID cryptographically links a signature to the certificate that should be used to validate it. It identifies the certificate by its hash, and that hash was hardwired to SHA-1.

Because of recent attacks on SHA-1, RFC 5035 defines the structure ESSCertIDv2, which includes an algorithm identifier, and a new attribute, SigningCertificateV2, that uses it. The old structure stays in use so that SHA-1 deployments remain compatible. The RFC updates Section 5.4 of RFC 2634 and replaces its ASN.1 module.
sections.eli5: A fingerprint check was built for just one kind of fingerprint, and that kind got easier to fake. Now the check can say which kind of fingerprint it uses.

sections.title: Which Attribute to Use
sections.content:
The signing certificate attribute is meant to prevent simple substitution and re-issue attacks, and to allow a restricted set of certificates to be used when verifying a signature. Two attributes exist because of a flaw in the original design. The main difference is that SigningCertificateV2 allows hash algorithm agility, while SigningCertificate forces SHA-1.

When SHA-1 is used, SigningCertificate MUST be used. SigningCertificateV2 MUST be used for any other algorithm and SHOULD NOT be used for SHA-1. Applications SHOULD recognize both as long as they consider SHA-1 able to tell two certificates apart. If both are present, they are evaluated independently.
sections.eli5: There are two forms: an old one that only knows one fingerprint type and a new one that can name any type. You use the old one for the old type and the new one for everything else.

sections.title: SigningCertificateV2 and ESSCertIDv2
sections.content:
SigningCertificateV2 has OID id-aa-signingCertificateV2 (arc value 47 under id-aa). It contains certs, a sequence of ESSCertIDv2, and optional policies. The first certificate in certs MUST be the one used to verify the signature, and if its hash does not match, the signature MUST be considered invalid. Later certificates, which can be attribute or public key certificates, limit the set used during validation.

Each ESSCertIDv2 has a hashAlgorithm (default id-sha256), a certHash and an optional issuerSerial. The hash is the way to confirm the verifier has the certificate the signer intended. The issuer and serial number pair is the usual identifier in RFC 3280, but the sid field in SignerInfo is not covered by the signature, so the pair SHOULD be placed in issuerSerial when it needs to be signed.

The attribute MUST be a signed attribute, never unsigned. A SignerInfo MUST NOT contain more than one instance, and it MUST have exactly one attribute value.

The RFC text says the certHash of ESSCertIDv2 is computed over the entire DER-encoded certificate, including its signature. The text also mentions SHA-1 in that field's description, although the structure's default algorithm is id-sha256.
sections.eli5: The signature carries a small card naming which fingerprint method was used and the fingerprint itself, so the checker can be sure it found the right certificate.

sections.title: Checking the Signature and the Hash
sections.content:
The RFC lists four outcomes when both the signature and the certificate hash are checked.

  • Signature valid, hashes match: success.
  • Signature valid, hashes do not match: the certificate has the right public key but is not the one the signer intended. The application should search for another certificate with the same public key whose hash matches, and otherwise it is a failure.
  • Signature invalid, hashes match: the signature is assumed modified, which is a failure.
  • Signature invalid, hashes do not match: either the signature was modified or the wrong certificate was used. The application should search for a certificate matching the hash and retry.
sections.eli5: You check two things: does the signature work, and is this the certificate the signer meant? Different combinations call for different next steps.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The goal is to stop a validator from using a substituted certificate. For example, an original certificate may have been revoked and a new one with the same public key issued to someone else. Since the issuer and serial number field is not protected, an attacker could point it at the new certificate and validation would succeed. The attributes must therefore sit in a signed location; elsewhere they add no security.

A poorly chosen hash algorithm may give inadequate protection or cause denial of service for this protection. Using the same hash as for message signing gives commensurate security and makes it likelier the recipient supports it. An unsupported hash for certificate identification does not stop the message from being validated but removes the protection against substitution.

Clients may include both ESSCertID and ESSCertIDv2 for legacy protection. If a signer has several certificates with the same public key, the two attributes could name different certificates, and recipients that evaluate both may choose to reject such a message.
sections.eli5: The fingerprint card only helps if it is locked inside the signed envelope. And a weak fingerprint method makes the card less useful.
